title: How to Review Construction Specs Division by Division: A GC Estimator's Workflow
summary: A division-by-division spec review workflow for GC estimators. Catch scope gaps before bid day. No manual read of 2,000 pages required.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- Most scope gaps are not random. They happen in predictable places across MasterFormat divisions.
- A division-by-division spec review catches missed trade scope, coordination gaps, and buried requirements before bid day.
- Six job types appear as flags in 39%–48% of scope packages, across every trade: embeds, sealants, blocking, temporary protection, testing, and firestopping.
- The highest-risk divisions for GCs are 03, 05, 07, 08, and the MEP cluster (21, 23, 26).
- The workflow below gives you a repeatable review sequence, with the specific items to look for in each division.


A construction spec set for a mid-size ICI project can run 1,500 to 2,000 pages. No estimator reads every word. The question is not whether you skip things. The question is whether you skip the right things.


Scope gaps that become change orders are rarely in the obscure sections. They are in the joints between trades. They are in the coordination items nobody owns. They are in spec requirements that assume a sub will infer the work.


A[structured division-by-division review](https://provision.com/blog) does not mean reading everything. It means knowing exactly where to look in each division, and reading those sections with discipline.


This workflow gives you that structure.


## Why Division-by-Division Review Matters More Than a Single Pass


A single linear read through a spec set is how items get missed. You are reading for scope, but the spec was written by an architect or engineer who was writing for compliance. Those are different documents with different purposes sitting in the same PDF.


When you read Division 03 with concrete in mind, you catch the grouting requirement on base plates. When you read Division 05 with steel in mind, you catch the embeds the concrete sub is supposed to cast. When you read them both with the interface in mind, you catch the gap between them.


That interface is where change orders live.


According to Provision's[Scope Gap Index](https://provision.com/scope-gap-index) , which tracked 1,290 scope packages across 24 projects from 16 general contractors in Q3 2026, 93% of packages had at least one flag from Scope Agent. Seventy-four percent had at least one coordination flag, meaning work between two trades that neither scope named.


The same six job types appeared across nearly every division: anchors and embeds, sealants and flashing joints, blocking and backing, temporary protection, testing and certification, and penetrations with firestopping. These are not exotic items. They are the standard hand-off points between trades, and they get dropped in almost every project.


## Before You Start: The Setup That Makes the Review Work


A division review is only as good as the document set going into it. Before you open the specs, do three things.


### 1. Confirm you have the full set


Check the table of contents against the issued drawings and addenda log. Missing spec sections are a common source of scope omissions. If Division 11 (Equipment) is in the drawings but not in the spec set, that is a gap before you start reviewing.


### 2. Pull the addenda first


Addenda frequently modify scope without revision clouding on drawings. Read each addendum for scope changes before you review the base spec. Otherwise you are building scope on superseded information.


### 3. Flag the coordination-heavy divisions upfront


Divisions 03, 05, 07, 08, and the MEP cluster are where most coordination gaps appear. Set a higher review threshold for those sections. That is where the dollar exposure concentrates.


## The Division-by-Division Review: Where to Look and What to Catch


### Division 01: General Requirements


Most estimators skim Division 01. That is a mistake. This is where project-wide cost obligations sit: temporary facilities, testing requirements, project closeout, and special inspections.


What to flag in Division 01:


- Testing and inspection requirements. Who provides them, who pays, and who schedules them. Per the Scope Gap Index, testing and certification was flagged in 47% of Division 01 packages.
- Temporary protection scope. Floor protection, weather barriers, and site fencing often appear here without a named responsible party.
- Coordination meeting requirements. If the spec requires weekly subcontractor coordination meetings, that is a GC cost.
- Closeout documentation obligations: O&M manuals, as-built drawings, commissioning records.


Write these requirements into your scope packages explicitly. Subs will not read Division 01 unless you tell them to.


### Division 02: Existing Conditions


Removal and demolition scope is frequently underspecified. The drawings show what gets demolished. The spec often does not say who hauls it, where it goes, or what happens to hazardous material.


The Scope Gap Index found removal, demolition, and disposal flagged in 63% of Division 02 packages across 22 projects.


What to flag in Division 02:


- Hazardous material abatement. Who scopes it, who does it, and what documentation is required.
- Disposal requirements: on-site stockpile, off-site disposal, or owner-retained salvage.
- Selective demolition interfaces with new work. The spec often leaves a gap between what gets removed and what the new trade starts with.


### Division 03: Concrete


Division 03 is one of the highest-risk divisions for coordination gaps. Concrete work touches nearly every other trade. Embeds, anchor bolts, sleeves, and blockouts are all cast at concrete time and owned by nobody unless a scope says otherwise.


Per the Scope Gap Index, anchors, embeds, and connections were flagged in 67% of Division 03 packages across 24 projects. That is the most-flagged item in the division.


A $45K stone-depth mismatch between civil, structural, and architectural drawings on a single slab is the kind of item a division review catches. The drawings conflict; the spec does not resolve it; the estimator who catches it before bid day qualifies the bid. The one who does not absorbs the cost.


What to flag in Division 03:


- Embeds and anchor bolts: who supplies, who sets, and who is responsible for location accuracy.
- Base plate grouting. Often called in Division 05 without scope in Division 03. It ends up in neither.
- Concrete pumping. The spec may require pump placement without saying who provides the pump.
- Slab-on-grade assembly conflicts between structural and architectural drawings.
- Penetration sleeves for MEP trades: who provides them and when.


### Division 05: Metals


Steel and miscellaneous metals scatter across multiple specs and multiple trades. The structural steel sub reads Division 05. The architectural metals sub reads whatever they think applies. The gap between them is where miscellaneous metals items go unpriced.


Anchors, embeds, and connections were flagged in 87% of Division 05 packages in the Scope Gap Index. That is the highest share of any item in any division tracked.


What to flag in Division 05:


- Miscellaneous metals: lintels, angle iron, pipe bollards, shelf angles. These often appear in the drawings but not in a named sub's scope.
- Hoisting and rigging. Who is responsible for unloading and setting steel elements that are not part of the structural package.
- Embeds in concrete: responsibility boundary between structural steel and concrete sub.
- Connections between structural and architectural steel: who details, who fabricates, who installs.


### Division 07: Thermal and Moisture Protection


Division 07 is where envelope continuity requirements live. The spec describes components. The drawings show configurations. Neither one names the person responsible for the joint between them.


Sealants, flashing, and waterproofing joints were flagged in 82% of Division 07 packages across 24 projects. The $400K missed roof cover board that one GC absorbed under "readily inferable" language was a Division 07 item. The spec required it. The drawings showed it. Nobody's scope said it.


What to flag in Division 07:


- Roof cover board: is it in the roofing spec, the insulation spec, or neither.
- Masonry-storefront flashing interfaces. Who stops and who starts at the frame.
- Interior vs. exterior caulking. The spec may require both under different sections with different subs assumed.
- Firestopping at envelope penetrations: who installs, who tests, and who certifies.
- Air barrier continuity at transitions between cladding systems.


The[Scope Gap Playbook's trade-specific chapter](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/trade-specific-scope-gaps) goes deeper on envelope gaps, including the masonry and storefront flashing patterns that repeat across ICI projects.


### Division 08: Openings


Doors, frames, hardware, and glazing each have their own spec sections and their own subs. The coordination requirements between them are where items fall through.


Openings, cutting, and patching were flagged in 66% of Division 08 packages.


What to flag in Division 08:


- Hollow metal door frames: who supplies and who installs. The drywall sub often assumes it is someone else.
- Hardware: is it in the door spec or a separate hardware spec. Who is responsible for final adjustment and hardware sets.
- Glazing warranty requirements: who is responsible for the full assembly vs. the glass unit alone.
- Cutting and patching for openings created by other trades. This often appears nowhere in any sub's scope.
- Fire-rated door certification: who tests and who maintains the certification documentation.


### Division 09: Finishes


Finish trades interact at every surface. The spec describes materials and application requirements. It rarely names the responsible party at trade interfaces.


What to flag in Division 09:


- Tolerance and flatness requirements for substrate trades. If the concrete does not meet FF/FL tolerances, who fixes it before the flooring sub installs.
- Gypcrete: it appears in some specs under Division 03, in others under Division 09. Confirm which sub is pricing it and that they know it by that name. Naming confusion between gypcrete and lightweight concrete has caused missed scope on multiple projects.
- Wall blocking for future fixtures: is it in this division, Division 06, or Division 10.
- Finish protection between trades: who is responsible for protecting finishes after installation and before turnover.


### MEP Cluster: Divisions 21, 22, 23, 26, 27, 28


MEP scope is where the most expensive coordination failures happen. Each trade has its own spec. Each spec was written independently. The coordination requirements across them are rarely explicit.


Testing and certification was flagged in 86% of Division 23 packages and 89% of Division 26 packages. These are not obscure requirements. They are the air balance report, the pressure test, and the megger test that the spec requires and that never appears in any sub's scope unless you put it there.


What to flag across the MEP cluster:


- Generator field conditioning: who is responsible for testing and conditioning on site. This has generated disputed costs across multiple projects. It almost never appears in anyone's scope.
- Motor starters: are they in the electrical spec, the mechanical spec, or both. Duplication and omission both happen.
- Fire-rated louvres: who supplies, who installs, who provides the fire damper certification.
- Lighting controls: who provides the control system, who programs it, and who commissions it.
- The trench: who excavates for underground MEP, who backfills, who compacts, and who is responsible for restoration.
- Testing, balancing, and commissioning for each system: who schedules, who witnesses, and who signs the report.


As one Pre-Construction Lead at a Top-ENR Canadian GC put it: "If you miss anything, they'll bill it." MEP subs in 2026 are faster than ever to submit change orders on scope that was not explicitly written into their package.


## The Six Items That Appear in Every Division


Provision's Scope Gap Index identified six job types flagged in 39%–48% of all 1,290 scope packages it reviewed, across every trade. These are the items to check in every division, not just the ones listed above.


Job Type Share Flagged (of 1,290 packages) Typical Gap Pattern


Anchors, embeds and connections 48% Drawing shows the embed. Neither scope says who buys or sets it.


Sealants, flashing and waterproofing joints 45% Interface between two cladding subs. Neither scope covers the joint.


Blocking, backing and support 44% Millwork sub assumes blocking is there. Drywall sub never priced it.


Temporary protection 42% Finished floor needs covering. No scope names who does it.


Testing, inspection and certification 40% Spec requires the test. No sub has it in their number.


Penetrations, sleeves and firestopping 39% Pipe goes through rated wall. Who sleeves, seals, and certifies is unwritten.


These six items represent the structural gaps between trades. A checklist written trade by trade will not catch them, because the item was never on one trade's list to begin with. It lives in the gap between two lists, and nobody owns the gap.


## Common Anti-Patterns That Undermine a Spec Review


Even with the right workflow, certain habits defeat the review before it starts. The[Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook) , built from 200+ GC interviews, names the patterns that repeat across firms and projects.


- **"As per plans and specs."** This is the most common anti-pattern in scope writing. It transfers risk to the GC under "readily inferable" language. If the sub can argue the item was not explicitly in their scope, the GC absorbs it.
- **Copy-paste from the previous similar job.** Last year's hospital scope is not this hospital's scope. Division references, spec numbers, and coordination requirements change with every set.
- **Junior estimators stuffing previous scopes verbatim.** Items that did not apply last time still appear. Items specific to this project never get added.
- **The five-minutes-before-bid review.** A scope review run as a final check on bid day catches nothing that matters. The review has to happen early enough to write what you find into the packages you send subs.


The fix for each of these is a structured review run early, not a final read-through run late. The[Scope Gap Playbook's chapter on subcontract language](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/subcontract-language-scope) covers how to write what you find into scope packages that hold up in the field.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### How long does a division-by-division spec review take for a mid-size ICI project?


A thorough manual review of a 1,500-to-2,000-page spec set takes two to four days for an experienced estimator. The review time compresses significantly when you use a structured checklist per division and focus on the highest-risk sections: Divisions 03, 05, 07, 08, and the MEP cluster.


### Which MasterFormat divisions carry the most scope gap risk?


Divisions 03 (Concrete), 05 (Metals), 07 (Thermal and Moisture Protection), 08 (Openings), and the MEP cluster (Divisions 21, 23, 26) carry the highest coordination gap risk. Per Provision's Scope Gap Index, embed, sealant, and testing items were flagged in 67%–96% of packages in those divisions across 24 projects.


### What is the most common spec review anti-pattern among GC estimators?


Writing "as per plans and specs" in a subcontractor scope package is the most common anti-pattern. It transfers scope risk to the GC under readily inferable contract language. If the item is not explicitly named in the sub's scope, the GC absorbs the cost when it surfaces as a change order.


### How do I catch coordination gaps between two trades in the spec review?


Read the two adjacent divisions together, not sequentially. When reviewing Division 03 and Division 05, look for items one spec assumes the other will cover: embeds, anchor bolts, and base plate grouting are the most common. Flag any item where both specs assume the other trade is responsible.


### Should addenda be reviewed before or after the base spec?


Review addenda before the base spec. Addenda modify scope, clarify requirements, and sometimes reverse base-spec requirements. Building scope from the base spec and then layering addenda creates errors. Read addenda first so the base spec review reflects the current document set.


### What is the "readily inferable" risk in construction specs?


Readily inferable language means a contract or spec requires work that is not explicitly named, on the basis that an experienced contractor should have known it was needed. A $300K lead-lined glass omission absorbed by a GC under this language is a documented example. The fix is to name every item explicitly in the subcontractor scope package.


### How does AI spec review compare to manual review for GC estimators?


AI tools like Provision's[Scope Agent](https://provision.com/scope-agent) read the full digital document set together and generate trade-specific scope packages with source citations. Scope Agent matched scope items at 97.01% accuracy on Provision's internal validation dataset, compared to 91.3% for a human estimator on the same exercise. The primary advantage is speed and coverage across a large document set.
